# Appendix A: Literature review {#sec-app-literature .appendix}

This appendix reviews the literature by theme. Where only an abstract or the bibliographic record could be checked, the text says what a work addresses rather than what it finds.

**A.1 Destination and origin bases, and VAT.** VAT is levied on the destination basis: the tax on a good or service accrues where it is consumed, with exports relieved and imports charged [@OECD2017VAT]. The equivalence of origin- and destination-based commodity taxes is old: for a uniform, broad-based tax, switching the basis changes price levels and exchange rates but not real allocations [@LockwoodDeMezaMyles1994]. @LockwoodWhalley2010 apply the result to carbon border adjustments and argue that the policy debate confuses price-level effects with relative-price effects. The result cuts both ways for this paper. It explains why the VAT machinery adjusts for borders without extra apparatus, which is the practical case for using it. It also shows that VAT's value component, being uniform, carries no carbon incentive and no trade advantage: everything that matters for carbon and for trade sits in the carbon component. The World Bank's total carbon price takes the same view: @Agnolucci2023 compute direct and indirect carbon prices for 142 countries over 1991–2021 and exclude general VAT because, as across-the-board consumption taxes, VATs "do not affect relative prices"; only VAT preferences on fuels enter, as subsidies. The arithmetic that a 15 percent VAT on a good embodying 0.30 kg per euro is "worth" €500 per tonne is correct, but it is not a carbon price in any useful sense.

VAT's spread is documented by @KeenLockwood2010. Destination-based business taxation rests on the same logic as VAT: a tax levied where the immobile consumer is removes the incentive to shift profits or production [@Auerbach2017]. @Shapiro2021 adds an observation that sharpens the case for a destination charge on carbon: tariffs and non-tariff barriers are lower on dirty industries than on clean ones, which amounts to an implicit global subsidy to CO₂ in traded goods of \$550–800 billion a year. The existing destination-side tax on trade already prices embodied carbon negatively.

**A.2 Consumption-based accounting.** Production-based inventories, which national targets use, attribute emissions to the country where they occur; consumption-based accounts attribute them to the country of final demand [@PetersHertwich2008]. Emissions from producing traded goods grew from 4.3 GtCO₂ (20 percent of the global total) in 1990 to 7.8 GtCO₂ (26 percent) in 2008, and net transfers from developing to developed countries grew from 0.4 to 1.6 GtCO₂, more than the Kyoto Protocol's reductions [@Peters2011]. In 2004, 23 percent of global CO₂ was embodied in trade, and more than 30 percent of consumption-based emissions were imported in Switzerland, Sweden, Austria, the United Kingdom and France [@DavisCaldeira2010]. @Grubb2022 find that net transfers peaked around 2006 and have declined since.

Two qualifications matter. @JakobSteckelEdenhofer2014 argue that a tonne of imported embodied emissions is not a tonne added to global emissions, so pricing all embodied carbon at the full social cost is not first-best; trade measures should concentrate on a few emissions-intensive, highly traded industries. And @Steininger2014 compare the justice and cost-effectiveness of consumption- and production-based approaches for a region acting alone. This paper therefore rests the case for a consumption charge on leakage, administration and acceptability, not on first-best optimality (@sec-objections).

**A.3 Carbon-added taxes, footprint taxes and consumption charges.** The carbon-added tax was proposed for Canada by @CourcheneAllan2008: a destination-based tax that, like a VAT, rebates the carbon tax on inputs so that only the carbon added at each stage is carried forward, with imports taxed at entry and exports relieved [@CourcheneAllan2011]. @McLure2010 replied that carbon content is unobservable, that extending a credit-method tax through retail would impose compliance and administrative costs out of proportion to the gain, and that border adjustments on imports would need the same ad hoc methods as other carbon taxes; he preferred an upstream tax with border adjustments limited to a few carbon- and trade-intensive basic products. @McAuslandNajjar2015 analyze a carbon footprint tax modeled on a credit-method VAT. They find a pure version, which requires the footprint of every product, possibly too costly, and propose a hybrid in which firms either calculate their own footprints or use default footprints for their product class; because it falls on all goods consumed at home, it keeps domestic firms on an equal footing with producers in countries without climate policy. @EichnerPethig2015 show that a unilateral consumption-based carbon tax can produce negative leakage in general equilibrium.

A European proposal for a consumption charge on carbon-intensive materials, sometimes called a climate contribution, is the nearest policy relative. @Ismer2016 set out its legal design as an excise-like charge at product-specific benchmark intensity, applying equally to imports. @PollittNeuhoffLin2020 simulate it with the E3ME model: with the charge rising to about €80 per tonne by 2050, it cuts EU CO₂ emissions by up to 10 percent by 2050 and, because imports are charged alike, avoids leakage. @Grubb2022 place the charge among three trade-compatible price options (border adjustments, a carbon-footprint consumption charge, and an excise contribution combined with free allocation). They note that a charge on actual footprints would reward exporters who decarbonize, but that tracing embodied carbon through global value chains is administratively demanding and open to fraud; defaults by product category are a feasible shortcut if they apply to imports and domestic goods alike. @Neuhoff2026 restate the idea for the CBAM era: CBAM's production-specific intensities invite resource shuffling, as foreign producers send their cleanest output to the EU; they propose a standardized liability per tonne of material, independent of process and origin, applied along the value chain with export relief.

@Holland2012 shows that, when regulation is incomplete and leakage is possible, an intensity standard combined with a consumption tax can sometimes reach the first best, and @BoehringerRosendahlStorrosten2017 that output-based rebating combined with a consumption tax on emission-intensive, trade-exposed goods can be equivalent to a border carbon adjustment: the formal case for pairing the consumption track with an intensity-based production track. What this paper adds to the line is the chain results, the calibration for a whole household basket, the swap inside VAT, and the deduction that links the consumption track to the production track.

**A.4 Border adjustment, trade law and trading partners.** The design literature establishes the main choices for border carbon adjustment: sectoral coverage, the measure of embodied carbon (domestic benchmark, country default or firm data), treatment of exports, and recognition of foreign policy [@IsmerNeuhoff2007; @Mehling2019; @KeenParryRoaf2022]. @Mehling2019 give the fullest legal analysis, under GATT Articles I, II:2(a), III and XX and the Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures, and recommend narrow coverage, default values with a right of rebuttal and crediting of foreign policies; they leave open whether carbon intensity can differentiate like products under Article III:2. @IsmerNeuhoff2007 argue that border adjustment at the intensity of the best available technology is defensible. @KeenParryRoaf2022 recommend benchmarking first on domestic intensities and moving to country-specific values later, with rebuttal, and note the tension between destination-basis border adjustment and the origin-basis accounting of the Paris Agreement.

The evidence on trading partners favors one default for every origin. @Mattoo2009 find that a border tax on the carbon content of imports, measured at the exporter's own intensity across all merchandise, would cut China's manufacturing exports by about a fifth and low- and middle-income countries' exports by 8 percent, while a tax based on the carbon content of domestic production would do far less damage. @CBAMExposure2025 find macroeconomic exposure to CBAM small for most countries and high for a few; their method could size partners' exposure to an economy-wide carbon component. @Evans2021 show that a border adjustment on imports alone leaves exporters exposed and that export relief raises legal risk, which careful design can reduce; a VAT-based charge zero-rates exports by construction.

**A.5 Leakage.** Model-based studies find leakage of 5–25 percent without border adjustment, and some leakage survives border adjustment through the fossil-fuel price channel [@BrangerQuirion2014]. Ex-post studies find no detectable leakage from the EU ETS so far [@NaegeleZaklan2019; @Dechezlepretre2022], partly because industry was shielded by free allocation [@Grubb2022]. Two consequences follow. The claim that a destination charge is leakage-proof holds for the goods channel only. And the case for a consumption charge concerns the carbon prices of €100–200 per tonne in prospect, not the leakage observed at the prices of the past.

**A.6 Distribution and acceptability.** Household carbon is a necessity. Environmental Engel curves for the United States show household CO₂ rising with income but less than proportionally [@Sager2019], and the same holds for local air pollutants, with curves shifting down over time [@LevinsonOBrien2019]. A uniform per-tonne charge on consumption therefore takes a larger share of poorer households' spending before revenue is returned. VAT itself is regressive against income but proportional or progressive against total spending [@Decoster2010]. The most directly relevant study is @Feindt2021, who model a comprehensive carbon price on all goods, including imported ones, in 23 EU countries: incidence before recycling is mostly neutral, sometimes progressive, within countries, but regressive across the EU, because households in lower-income, mainly eastern, member states bear higher average burdens; relatively small transfers between member states would offset this. @sec-distribution reproduces both patterns with independent data.

Acceptability depends on perceptions as much as on incidence. After the Yellow Vests protests, most French respondents rejected a tax-and-dividend scheme, overestimated their own losses and wrongly believed it regressive, and information moved beliefs only slightly [@DouenneFabre2022]. Across 20 countries, support for climate policies depends on perceived effectiveness, perceived personal losses and concern for poorer households [@Dechezlepretre2025]. @Carattini2018 identify five sources of resistance to carbon taxes (personal cost, regressivity, economic damage, doubts about effectiveness and suspicion of a revenue grab) and remedies including phasing, earmarking, lump-sum rebates and communication; @Klenert2018 review how revenue use shapes public support. A revenue-neutral swap phased over ten years answers the revenue-grab and personal-cost concerns; presenting it as a cut in VAT on clean goods answers the effectiveness concern.

**A.7 Credibility and forward commitment.** Optimal plans are time-inconsistent when agents' expectations depend on future policy [@KydlandPrescott1977]. @HelmHepburnMash2003 apply the problem to carbon and propose delegating carbon policy to an independent agency; @Brunner2012 compare commitment devices, including legislation, delegation, contracts and reputation; @Nemet2017 set out remedies for credibility problems in low-carbon investment and their advantages and drawbacks. @ChiappinelliNeuhoff2020 show that carbon contracts for difference, in which the government pays investors a fixed carbon price, improve decarbonization incentives and derive conditions under which the government is willing to tie its hands. On instrument choice, exogenous pricing through a tax or a cap with a price floor or ceiling avoids price volatility and harmful interactions with other policies [@GoulderSchein2013]. The forward obligation of @sec-obligation applies these ideas to ETS2: it is an application, not a new mechanism, and its novelty is the published floor fixed a decade ahead.

**A.8 Feebates and the production track.** Feebates price intensity without raising average costs. @SternerIsaksson2006 analyze Sweden's refunded NOₓ charge, a working revenue-neutral feebate, and @DHaultfoeuille2014 find that France's car bonus-malus shifted purchases toward low-CO₂ cars but raised total CO₂ emissions, because it also raised car sales: a lesson on benchmark design. Intensity standards, the regulatory cousin of feebates, implicitly subsidize output and can even raise emissions [@HollandHughesKnittel2009]; the consumption track exists to supply the output margin they miss [@CFPB11; @CFPB12].

# Appendix B: Proofs {#sec-app-proofs .appendix}

*Setup.* Stages $k = 1, \dots, n$; $p_k = p_{k-1} + w_k$ with $p_0 = 0$; $E_k = \sum_{j=1}^{k} a_j$ with $E_0 = 0$; carbon base $C_k$ with $C_0 = 0$; remittance $T_k$ as in @eq-remit. Prices are cost plus value added; taxes are passed to the next stage, except that an exempt firm's irrecoverable input taxes become part of its price.

*Proposition 1.* (i) $\sum_{k=1}^{n} T_k = v \sum_{k=1}^{n} (p_k - p_{k-1}) + P \sum_{k=1}^{n} (C_k - C_{k-1}) = v\,p_n + P\,C_n$, because both sums telescope; nothing depends on $C_1, \dots, C_{n-1}$. (ii) With $C_k = E_k$, the carbon part of $T_k$ is $P(E_k - E_{k-1}) = P\,a_k$. (iii) The consumer pays $p_n + v\,p_n + P\,C_n$; with $C_n = E_n$ the carbon part is $P\,E_n$. Under carry-forward, $C_k = C_{k-1} + a_k$ for every $k$ from the first verified stage on, so a verified base upstream reaches $C_n$ and hence the consumer price.

*Proposition 2.* Let stage $j$ be exempt. It remits nothing and pays $v\,p_{j-1} + P\,C_{j-1}$ to its supplier without credit, so its price is $p^x_j = p_{j-1} + w_j + v\,p_{j-1} + P\,E_{j-1}$ when $C_{j-1} = E_{j-1}$. (i) If $j = n$, the consumer pays $p^x_n = p_n + v\,p_{n-1} + P\,E_{n-1}$ and no further tax. Against full crediting, $(1+v)\,p_n + P\,E_n$, the difference is $-v\,w_n - P\,a_n$: value added and carbon added at the exempt stage go untaxed, and upstream carbon is charged once. (ii) If $j < n$, every later price is higher by $\Delta = v\,p_{j-1} + P\,E_{j-1}$, and stage $j+1$ has no creditable input tax, so the taxes on later invoices are $v$ and $P\,C_k$ on the full values and bases. The consumer pays $(1+v)(p_n + \Delta) + P\,E_n$, which exceeds the full-crediting outlay by $(1+v)\,\Delta = (1+v)(v\,p_{j-1} + P\,E_{j-1})$. The upstream carbon $E_{j-1}$ is charged once inside $\Delta$ and again inside $E_n$.

*Proposition 3.* With $Q_k = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \min(q_j, P)\, a_j$ and carbon component $P\,E_k - Q_k$ on each sale, firm $k$ remits $(P\,E_k - Q_k) - (P\,E_{k-1} - Q_{k-1}) = (P - \min(q_k, P))\,a_k \ge 0$. Each tonne emitted at stage $k$ bears $q_k$ directly and $P - \min(q_k, P)$ through the carbon component, a total of $\max(P, q_k)$. Summed over the chain, the carbon component raises $P\,E_n - Q_n$ and explicit prices raise $\sum_{k=1}^{n} q_k a_k$, which equals $P\,E_n$ when every $q_k \le P$. For a revenue-neutral feebate the sector-average net price is zero, so it contributes nothing to $Q$ and the consumer bears $P\,E_n$ through the carbon component. With default bases $C_k$ in place of $E_k$, $P\,C_k - Q_k$ can be negative when the default understates an ETS-heavy chain; flooring the charge at zero keeps every remittance from becoming a refund on that account.

All three results were checked symbolically for $n = 4$ with sympy, and the worked example of @sec-chain numerically, in `2.Source/check_propositions.py`.

![Value component, ETS price and carbon component remitted at each stage of the worked example in @sec-chain. Source: `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py`.](2.Source/figures/fig4-vat-chain.png){#fig-chain width=90%}

# Appendix C: Calibration of defaults and distribution {#sec-app-calibration .appendix}

*Data.* (1) FIGARO inter-country input–output table at basic prices, product by product, 2022, million euro [@EurostatFIGARO]: 50 economies (45 named countries plus the rest of the world and four Western Balkan economies) by 64 CPA products, with five categories of final demand. (2) Greenhouse gas emissions by emitting country and NACE A*64 industry, thousand tonnes CO₂e, from the footprint dataset with destination "world" and all final demand [@EurostatGHGFP]; the CO₂-only dataset gives the last column of @tbl-defaults. (3) Household direct emissions from heating and transport [@EurostatAEA]. (4) Household budget shares by income quintile, 2020 wave, and mean expenditure by quintile [@EurostatHBS]. (5) Household final consumption by COICOP purpose, 2022 [@EurostatCOICOP]. All were downloaded from the Eurostat API on 29 October 2026.

*Model.* With intermediate flows $Z$, output $x$ and technical coefficients $A = Z \hat{x}^{-1}$, emission intensities per euro of output $s = f \hat{x}^{-1}$, where industry emissions $f$ are assigned to the matching CPA product, the multipliers are $m = s\,(I - A)^{-1}$, in kg CO₂e per euro of final demand. The four Western Balkan economies, present in FIGARO but not in the emissions data, take the rest-of-world intensity for each product; they are a negligible share of EU purchases. Category intensities weight $m$ by EU-27 household final consumption by origin and product. The model gives an EU-27 footprint of 3,749 Mt CO₂e for all final demand excluding households' direct emissions, against Eurostat's 3,743 Mt; for households alone, 2,282 Mt against 2,255 Mt; for CO₂ alone, 2,760 Mt against 2,797 Mt.

*Purchasers' prices.* Household purchases of trade services (CPA G45–G47), €1.19 trillion, are 64.5 percent of household purchases of goods (CPA A–C) at basic prices, €1.85 trillion. Spreading them evenly gives a goods intensity at purchasers' prices of $(e_g + 0.645\, e_{\text{trade}})/1.645$. Taxes on products are excluded throughout.

*Sources of the footprint.* Of the 2,116 Mt CO₂e embodied in taxable household purchases, 28 percent was emitted by EU power and energy-intensive industry (CPA D35, C17, C19, C20, C23, C24, a proxy for ETS coverage), 14 percent by EU agriculture, 17 percent by other EU industries and services, and 40 percent outside the EU (`2.Source/footprint_sources.csv`).

*Distribution.* COICOP 3-digit purposes are mapped to the categories of @tbl-defaults (`2.Source/distribution.py`); rents, health and education services, social protection, insurance and finance are exempt. Household energy (COICOP 04.5) carries the embodied intensity of electricity and gas supply per euro of EU spending on it, 0.83 kg CO₂e per euro; fuel for vehicles (07.2) carries the supply-chain intensity of refined petroleum products per euro of spending on it, 0.25 kg per euro. Direct emissions per euro of 04.5 and 07.2 spending are computed for each member state. Simplifications: budget shares are applied to spending including taxes; every member state uses EU-wide defaults; national quintiles are averaged with household-spending weights rather than ranked EU-wide; the 2020 survey wave is combined with 2022 intensities.

*Code.* `2.Source/calibrate_defaults.py` builds the model and writes `defaults_by_category.csv`, `defaults_by_product.csv`, `basket_summary.csv` and `footprint_sources.csv`; `2.Source/distribution.py` writes the distribution files; `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py` prints the fiscal numbers and draws @fig-defaults, @fig-rule, @fig-distribution and @fig-chain. The input–output download is about 72 MB and is cached outside the repository. Setting the environment variable `CCT_YEAR=2023` reruns the calibration for 2023, which gives a taxable basket intensity of 0.36 kg CO₂e per euro.
